utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Registrar. Will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel. And good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Ms. Tecla Henry-Benjamin, Daryl Mundis, and Andres Vatter, our case manager. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, lead counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Mirna Milanovic, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic and Mr. Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber bids good morning to all those present, the representatives of the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, the accused, as well as all the staff of this courtroom, a courtroom which we are working in after several days, but I must note that the model has disappeared. I hope it will reappear, because normally it should be in front of us and it is not there. We have a witness planned for this morning who should be at the disposal of the Chamber. Would the usher please go and fetch the witness. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. While the witness is being brought into the courtroom, as Your Honours are aware, there is an audiotape of an interview this witness conducted in August of 1992. The Prosecution, as I informed the legal officer yesterday, was intending on playing an excerpt of that tape so that the witness could properly authenticate it. Immediately prior to this morning's hearing, I was informed by Mr. Bourgon that the Defence would not object to the transcript and the tape going into evidence without any excerpt of it being played. And I'm simply wondering if the Chamber, for whatever reason, would like to hear a part of that tape. We're happy to do so. However, in light of what Mr. Bourgon informed me of earlier, it would appear that it would not be necessary for us to play that, in light of the fact that they will not object to the transcript and the tape being admitted into evidence once I've laid the proper foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will see if it's necessary to hear the tape during the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you stand, please. First may I ask you whether you're hearing me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are. Fine. You have been called by the Prosecution as a witness. Before reading the solemn declaration, I need to be able to identify you. For that purpose, will you please give me your first and last name, date and place of birth, and your nationality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Andrew Hogg. I'm British. I was born in London on the 18th of July, 1953.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I work as a press officer for the medical foundation for the care of victims of torture, which is a British charity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in 1993, what was your occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a foreign correspondent for The Sunday Times of London. Specifically, I was Middle East correspondent at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you were The Sunday Times correspondent. Have you testified before in an international or a national court about the events that took place in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is the first time for you to testify in court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you be kind enough to read the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before giving the floor to representatives of the Prosecution, I should like to provide some explanations regarding these proceedings. You will be requested to answer questions put to you by representatives of the Prosecution during the stage known as the examination-in-chief. Normally this stage can last between one and a half hours. When that stage of the proceedings has been completed, the counsel for the Defence, who are to your left, will also have questions for you as part of the cross-examination. The questions have two aims in mind, as envisaged by the Rules of Procedure, and that is to verify the credibility of the witness and also to provide elements regarding the context within which the facts took place, from the standpoint of the Defence. Upon the completion of the cross-examination, the Prosecution may have some additional questions for you in the light of what answers you gave in the course of the cross-examination. The three Judges, who are here in front of you, may also have questions for you at any stage of the proceedings, but it is customary for the Judges to wait for the examination-in-chief, the cross-examination, and the re-examination to be completed, and only then to ask you questions, the aim being either to clarify your answers or to fill in any grey areas or missing points in your answers. Upon the completion of the Judges' questions, the Defence counsel and the Prosecution may also have some additional questions. Try and answer the questions as completely, as precisely as possible, even though you will be asked about events that took place more than ten years ago, but to the extent that you remember, try and be clear and precise. If questions seem to be too complicated for you, ask the person asking them to rephrase them in clearer and more precise terms. Finally, let me tell you two other points, which normally should not apply to you, but as you are a witness, like all others, it is my duty to tell witnesses that as you have taken the solemn declaration to tell the whole truth, this means that all forms of false testimony are excluded, as any false testimony can be prosecuted, as the Rules of this Tribunal envisage a penalty up to seven years of imprisonment and, in addition, a pecuniary fine. However, the Rules also provide for the possibility of a witness not answering a question, should the answers contain elements that could be used against him. In such a case, the Chamber may compel the witness to answer but at the same time the Chamber guarantees the witness in that case a form of immunity. So those would be, in very general terms, how these proceedings will evolve. Should you encounter any difficulty, please do not hesitate to address the Chamber. I'll now turn to the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor. I don't know who's going to be the person asking questions. I think it's Mr. Mundis. Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogg, you've told the Chamber that you were the Middle East correspondent for The Sunday Times of London in 1993. Can you please tell us when you began that assignment.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I took over that role in 1991, at the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, can you tell us please when you first began working for The Sunday Times.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I started working for The Sunday Times in 1984 on a full-time basis. Prior to that, I had been doing what's known as casual shifts, from about 1980 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about what your responsibilities were as the Middle East correspondent for The Sunday Times.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Specifically I had to keep a -- a close eye on developments in Israel and the occupied territories, but at that time there were a number of other big stories going on. The -- the first assignment I took in late 1991 was to go to Lebanon, where the last of the hostages were just being released. I spent some three weeks there interviewing people from Hezbollah, which would have been unthinkable some months earlier. I went to Algeria at the beginning of 1992 for the beginning of what turned into a civil war there. I was in Afghanistan when -- well, just after Najibullah had been deposed, so I was there when the Mujahedin took over. I travelled overland disguised as a member of the Mujahedin to enter Kabul. I had been by that time as well to Northern Iraq, where the first elections among the Kurds were taking place. From memory, I think I'd also been in Jordan by that time and probably into Southern Iran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogg, did there come a time in 1992 when you went to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: There certainly did, yeah, in the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber why the Middle East correspondent for The Sunday Times would go to Bosnia, which wouldn't seem to be part of the Middle East.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Right. Following the Middle East peace conference in Madrid in autumn of 1991, the region in a sense, particularly the Israeli-Palestinian dispute, seemed to go quiet. We found out the reason later; there were meetings taking place in a farmhouse outside Oslo which nobody but the participants knew about. As such, I was anxious obviously to -- to continue appearing in the newspaper. As the Bosnian conflict unfolded, it became clear to me that because of the persecution of the Muslims in Bosnia, that that was a story which would have ramifications throughout the region I covered. So I volunteered to go to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you entered Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: From where did you enter Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: From Split. I'd flown to Zagreb, travelled down from Zagreb to Split by ferry, and then entered Bosnia from Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you receive any information when you were in Zagreb that allowed you to focus your attention or what you were interested in covering in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Not in Zagreb. When I reached Split -- I had heard rumours, I can't remember from where, that there were members of the Mujahedin in Bosnia. When I was in Split, I asked a -- a liaison officer, if you like, for a local Croat politician who was -- the liaison officer was Australian, and I asked him, "Where are the Mujahedin?" And he replied, "You're best going to Travnik to find the answer to that."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At approximately what month in 1992 was it that you entered Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: It has to be in August. I thought originally that it was late July, but going back over it in my mind, it was -- it was definitely August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This liaison officer indicated to you that you should go to Travnik. What -- where in fact did you go?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: To Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber how you got to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah. I travelled with a photographer and a young Croatian interpreter in a Lada Niva.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of the photographer you travelled with?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: The photographer was Simon Townsley.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber about your arrival in Travnik. Approximately what time of day you got there. Do you recall the specific date?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I don't recall the specific date. What happened was we spent either two to three days in that region trying to find the Mujahedin, and various events that took place in that period of time I'm a little unsure of the chronology. I can outline, if you like, the events in total which -- which led to the interview with the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could you please do so, from the beginning with the time you arrived in Travnik and where you went.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: On arrival in Travnik, the first thing that we would have done, because it was standard, was to find the local army presence, if you like, to introduce ourselves and to get permission to travel around the region. In -- in dealing with the Bosnian army in Travnik at that time, they had what appeared to be a command post close to a waterfall. The reception we got was very civil, and we asked about the Mujahedin, and the response was that it would be entirely up to them if they wanted to talk to us. At some stage I was informed that members of the Mujahedin were staying in a house close to the painted wooden mosque in the centre of Travnik. I visited the house, but it was empty; there was no one there. We went back several times. While in Travnik, we went then to Turbe, which is a little hamlet just outside Travnik, slightly to the north of Travnik, because we had been told the Mujahedin were there. Turbe was under heavy mortar bombardment throughout the hour or so that we spent there. We were talking to Bosnian army officers who were in a room that was -- next to them there was a room full of HVO soldiers. We didn't have anything to do with them. We were concentrating on the Bosnian forces at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Sorry. They --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogg, if I could just briefly interrupt you at this point. When you tell us that Turbe was under heavy mortar bombardment, do you know which parties were involved in the armed conflict in August of 1992 when you were there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean, the mortar bombardment was from the Serbs, who were slightly to the north of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You also have told us about speaking to Bosnian army officers next to a room full of HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the time you were present in August of 1992, did you become aware of any relationship between HVO soldiers and Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina soldiers? And if so, can you tell the Chamber a little bit about what you observed and what you became aware of.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I was surprised -- I was under the impression that -- that there was a unity, if you like, between the Croat and the Bosnian soldiers facing a common threat from the Serbs. I was therefore surprised when I reached Turbe to suddenly realise that in fact it wasn't -- it didn't appear to be a unified command, which was something that I -- I thought a lot about, which is why subsequently when trying to find the Mujahedin I decided we'd probably be better off talking to members of the HVO, because the -- the Bosnians -- the Bosnian army people that we had met had been --"reluctance" is too strong a word, but they had been less than enthusiastic to set up any kind of meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that it didn't appear that there was a unified command. Can you characterise in any way the relationship between the HVO and the ABiH? Was it a hostile? Was it a friendly? Was it just that they had two different commands? How can you -- if you know, how can you characterise this relationship, in light of the fact that they faced a common foe in the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I didn't really have that much to do with -- let me start that again. It wasn't something that I was in a position to become an expert on. All I -- all I could do was observe, observing the -- the split at Turbe, observing the -- different checkpoints were manned by people from both parties, if you like. And there was no overt hostility, but I certainly sensed a tension there, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, when I interrupted you, I believe you were telling us about the -- your arrival in Turbe, which at that point was under mortar bombardment.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please pick up from -- from Turbe.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah. There was -- the bombardment was intense. It was so intense that it would have been foolhardy in the extreme to go out wandering about up to the front line which is close by. And by the same token we had been told by the Bosnians there at that post that there were no Mujahedin in the area. So we went back to Travnik, and I think at some stage the following morning there was a Serb air raid on a factory at Novi Travnik. We were at the hospital in Travnik, and the first we knew about this was when cars began appearing with badly wounded people in them. So we went immediately, myself, the photographer, and the interpreter, to Novi Travnik, where -- well, we could see that, you know, the burning factory. And we went to the HVO post there, the HVO post, and got the story, if you like, of what had taken place. Sometime a bit later in the conversation the question of the Mujahedin came up, and somebody in the HVO suggested Zenica was the place to go and look. If I could explain that it wasn't -- I was very keen on finding the Mujahedin, but the -- the reason was not just purely out of, you know, sort of journalistic interest. If you work for a Sunday newspaper, you have to find your own stories. You can't follow the daily day-to-day news because you're always going to be overtaken by your colleagues on daily newspapers. So it was the pursuit of an exclusive that meant that we drove then to Zenica. And having been given information in Novi Travnik by the HVO, we went to the HVO in Zenica and said, "What can you tell us about the Mujahedin here?" They had a debate among themselves as to whether they should, I suppose, tell us what they knew, but they ultimately decided to do so. I think that -- I mean, what -- what they did was direct us to an old people's home down by the river in Zenica as being the place where we would find the foreign fighters. They told us that they were becoming increasingly alarmed by the appearance in the town of men driving up-to-date 4 by 4s with good communications equipment who were clearly not Bosnian. So we went to the old people's home; by this time it was sort of early afternoon, and it was empty, except for a group of Bosnian soldiers who confirmed that there were Mujahedin staying at this particular property but that they were aware at the front line, and we couldn't really find out which front line or where. They told me that if I wanted further information, I should call a Bosnian officer. I'm afraid I don't recall his name, but I think in my statement there is a couple of possibilities mentioned. It was -- it was very clear to me that -- that the Bosnians at the old people's home were there as minders, if you like, for the Mujahedin and that the -- by providing me with this number, it indicated to me that -- that there was formal, official recognition by the Bosnian forces of the Mujahedin in that area. We -- having drawn a blank at the retirement home, we then travelled south to Visoko, which we knew was an active front line, to see whether we could find any of the fighters there. Visoko was also under very heavy bombardment, and we went to the local hospital where a woman doctor told me that a large number of Mujahedin had passed through just a few minutes earlier. I didn't actually believe her. I thought that -- she was very shaken. As I said, the bombardment outside was intense, and she was -- you know, she was -- she was clearly working all hours. After a while, we decided we were going to get nowhere there, so we pulled back to the Zenica region, and I think it was at a -- a checkpoint that once again we asked, "Where are the Mujahedin?" And somebody told us to go to the village of Mehurici. When we -- and this is -- by this time, it was quite late in the afternoon, and you don't want really to be travelling along unknown roads late in the day in Bosnia because you were concerned about the amount of alcohol the people at the checkpoints by that time would have drunk, so it was -- you know, it was getting time to find somewhere to -- to stay and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If I could just again interrupt briefly. Do you recall approximately where this checkpoint was?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah. It was -- it was somewhere between Zenica and Travnik on a -- you know, on a sort of back route. And we got to Mehurici, and the first thing that we did was -- was stop a passing woman and say, "Where are the Arabs?" And she just gestured up the hill. So we drove on up the hill almost sort of through the village, and we turned a corner and we saw a group of foreign fighters with a couple of men, clearly quite young men who I took to be Bosnian army. They were all engaged in what appeared to be washing some -- some new-looking 4 by 4s.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Hogg, if I could interrupt you. You mentioned "a couple of men clearly quite young who I took to be Bosnian army." Can you perhaps elaborate on that. Why did you reach that conclusion, and what do you mean by "young"?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: What I -- I reached that conclusion -- I can't be specific. It was a long time ago, but it had something to do with the insignia on their clothes, and it would have had something to do with the clothes they were wearing, which appeared to me to be, you know, regular Bosnian army issue, if you like. The reason that I mentioned that they were young is because my first instinct was that any Bosnian army person there was likely to prove obstructive, but I sort of -- taking in the scene as a glance, I realised that these -- that these two were really in a subordinate role. They appeared to be assistants or something like that. They certainly didn't appear to be in command of the people that they were with. I walked towards the group. We were a little bit above them on the road. They were just off the road, on a sort of a -- a bit of gravel or whatever. And I simply said, "Does anybody here speak English?" And much to my surprise, one of the foreign fighters detached himself from the group and said something along the lines of, "Yes, I do. How can I help you?" I explained to him that we had been searching for him for several days in quite difficult circumstances and that we felt that -- I felt that I wanted to tell his story, I wanted to explain why the Bosnian army had -- well, I wanted to explain why foreign fighters were in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, if I could again briefly interrupt you for some clarification. This individual who spoke English, did you subsequently determine his identity?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: He -- I mean, I asked him. I think he even introduced himself as Abdel Aziz.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please describe the appearance of Mr. Abdel Aziz. What -- what did he look like?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: From memory, he was -- he was not a large man. He was -- he was, you know, quite compact. I couldn't work out what his nationality was. I thought at first that he was probably from Pakistan. I was surprised at the quality of his English; it was good. And I -- I didn't really detect the kind of inflections that I -- I associate in Britain with people from Pakistan speaking English. So then I thought well, he was probably -- probably from an Arab country. He was dressed in sort of traditional Afghan dress, if you like, the -- I think it's called the "shalwar kameez," something of that nature. It's sort of baggy trousers, and over that -- and a tunic top. And over that he had a military coat; I think it was dark green from memory. I don't remember anything on his head. It wouldn't have been at all out of keeping if he had been wearing a "pakoul." He looked like a Mujahedin from Afghanistan. His hair and his beard were hennaed, which because of my travels in the Middle East by that time I recognised as being a sign that he was prepared to die in battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber about the other people that were in the group with Abdel Aziz.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean, it wasn't a large group. It was probably between six and ten, I would have thought. Most of them appeared to be in combat fatigues of some kind, camouflage trousers. One person stood out as wearing a kind of a grey jumpsuit or track-suit, something of that nature. He clearly wasn't Bosnian. He said absolutely nothing, of course. But the group looked like people that I had been in Afghanistan with just a few months earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you give us any kind of breakdown as to the appearance of the group between what would appear to you to be locals and what would appear to be foreign?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I can't -- from memory, it -- it seemed to me that the only local contingent were the two men I've mentioned, who -- you know, who appeared to be Bosnian military men. The rest of the group to me looked clearly foreign. And subsequently, when Abdel Aziz allowed us to take his photograph, one of the -- the conditions was we didn't take any pictures of any of these men. And that also accorded with what I'd experienced in -- in Afghanistan with the Arab Mujahedin there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you, Mr. Hogg, continue, please, with the discussion that you had with Mr. Abdel Aziz on this first occasion that you met him.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I explained to him that we were interested in -- in telling the world why the Mujahedin were there. I would have without doubt have told him that my sympathies were on the side of the Bosnian people. I -- I without doubt would have asked him where he was from, and I can't remember his precise answer, but he clearly wasn't going to discuss that. It was very short. It was -- and very civil. He simply said to me, "If you want an interview, come back here with permission from the Bosnian army. I will -- I will grant an interview if they allow it." My real concern was that between being able to get that permission and -- and getting the interview, he was going to vanish to a front line and we wouldn't be able to find him. By now it was -- it was early evening. We -- I'm pretty sure I found out from him that he wasn't planning to go anywhere that night and that he would be there first thing in the morning, because that was our only option was to go and get the permission and then go back there -- there the next day. So we drove very fast to Travnik to the army command post by the waterfall and we sent the female interpreter in to get the necessary permission, because we figured she had a better chance than we did. I wasn't expecting to get that permission at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, why -- why did you send the female interpreter into the building?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: She was young and good-looking and she spoke fluent what was known as Serbo-Croat at that time, and I -- she was -- she was an accomplished, I suppose, in journalist's terms you'd call it a fixer. She knew how to flatter people the right way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. And again, can you describe the building that she entered and what that building was being used for.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: The building, from memory, was either a -- formerly was either a restaurant or a restaurant with rooms to stay in. It clearly had been part of the Travnik tourist itinerary at some stage in the fairly recent past. It -- you know, it was quite a scenic place. There was the waterfall -- sorry, there was the waterfall rushing outside. I think there was -- from memory, there was a large tree there. It was -- it was clearly somewhere that tourists at some stage, you know, in the recent past had stopped to enjoy the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in August 1992, what was that building being used for?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: It seemed to me to be being used as a army command post. There was a sort of an operations room inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber how you -- you came to that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Because when we had been trying to find the Mujahedin the previous day and we had gone to this command post and we'd met with a woman officer, and she had told us, "Look --" we'd said, "If any of them come in, will you ask them if they will give us an interview?" And we were there later in the day when a very large Mujahedin fighter of Middle East appearance walked in. And so the lieutenant pleaded with her to ask him whether he'd give us an interview. And I observed -- I was able to observe from the door that there was, you know, there was communications equipment on the table, there were maps on the table. It was -- you know -- it was a command post of sorts. Anyway, the response from the Mujahedin fighter, who seemed to be very much at home there, was no. And I was told that he said something along the lines of, "This is my protest against the West," as a -- as his reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what happened after you sent your female interpreter into the building, then, on the following day?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Right. Well, she came out of the building clutching the paper. We were elated. We drove -- by now it was nightfall. We drove back to Kiseljak, which was some miles south, but where there was communications. There was a telex that we could use to talk to London, and there were rooms to stay in, and there was a restaurant to get something to eat. And then at first light we tore back to Mehurici, getting there well -- you know, sort of well before the 9.30 -- I'd made some kind of -- I said something to Abdel Aziz about something -- if we get back here by 9.30 or whatever, and he'd acquiesced to that. So we were there by about 8.30, I guess. We were there well early.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say "there," "we were there by about 8.30," where again are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: In Mehurici, the village itself. There was a little -- what from memory was a school, which seemed to be where the Mujahedin forces were based. And on the opposite side of the road there was a very rundown cafe. We didn't really want to attract too much attention to ourselves by, you know, sort of standing conspicuously around, for fear that somebody might come and negate the permission that we'd been given. So we went into the cafe and sat there for some time. By that time I had already gone to the gate and asked people to pass word in that we had the necessary permission and hat we were waiting outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long did you wait?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: From memory, it was about 40 minutes or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: When he came out, I immediately showed him the -- the piece of paper. He said something along the lines of, "Follow me." He got into a 4 by 4, we got into ours, and we followed him probably about half a mile up the hill until he turned off into -- into what was a field effectively with a stream at one end with woods screening the -- the stream from the field. And there were rocks in the field. And he got out, we got out, and -- before the interview began, I was -- I was concerned -- I didn't want anything to upset him. I didn't want -- I didn't want to cause him -- to bring it to a sudden halt, and so my first question was, "Where do you want the interpreter to sit?" And he gestured to some rocks quite some distance off. Actually, he clearly didn't want her anywhere near him, and so the interpreter moved some distance off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If I could again, Mr. Hogg, briefly interrupt you. What happened to the piece of paper once Mr. Abdel Aziz took that from you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I can't be certain. I believe he retained it, but I can't be certain, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, can you describe the number and types of people who were present on this morning.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Okay. There was myself, the interpreter, and Simon Townsley, the photographer. There was Abdel Aziz, and I recollect that there was -- he had two minders with him, both of them carrying AK-47s.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: These minders, as you've put them, did they appear to be foreign or did they appear to be local, and what were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: They appeared to be foreign. One of them was dressed in the kind of black or grey jumpsuit that I described earlier. He seemed to be -- his face was utterly impassive. He seemed to be very, very capable and very much at ease with his weapon, as indeed did the other one, but the one I've just mentioned was the most noticeable of the two. They took up sort of strategic positions, I suppose. One of them by the entrance to the field and the other one on a little crop of rocks quite close where we were sitting. It was -- part of me thought this was, you know, over the top but another part of me thought, you know, well, if you had received training of some kind, you know, this is what -- this is what you would -- you would see, people -- when I've come across, you know, sort of special forces soldier, even in innocuous places, there is a sort of a -- a forward behaviour. And these guys seemed to me to know what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please pick up with where you were when I interrupted you; that is, placing yourself and Mr. Aziz and Mr. Townsley at this location.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Aziz sat down on an outcrop of rocks, I sat down next to him, took out the tape recorder. I'm pretty sure I would have asked him permission to record, but I took a shorthand note of the interview as well, and then we got underway. It was a typical press interview. The -- I wanted to extract as much information out of him as possible, but I also knew that the story would only have half the impact if it didn't have a photograph with it. And I also knew that I couldn't ask for a photograph immediately. I had to develop some kind of rapport with him and build up a kind of relationship. So the questioning started. When I got what I deemed to be enough to write the story, although not as much as I wanted, we then broached the subject of the pictures. And as I expected, that took a little bit of negotiation. But ultimately, he agreed to have his picture taken, which I also was relatively surprised by. Once that had been accomplished, I then went back and continued the questioning for a little longer to get -- to get everything out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately how long did the interview take?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I would think probably just over half an hour, in that region.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was the reason that the interview concluded?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Abdel Aziz had made it very clear at the outset that his time was limited. As the interview progressed, you can -- you can just pick up small signs when somebody is growing impatient, and I certainly began picking up those signs. His -- his impatience grew at about the time that his minders' impatience grew, and in the end one of them said to him along the lines of, you know, "You've got to be going," or something like that, and so he brought the interview to a sudden close then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What did Mr. Abdel Aziz do at the conclusion of the interview?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I -- I really can't remember. I would have imagined that we shook hands and got into our respective vehicles and then we drove the fastest we could away from Mehurici. We had to reach the coast to -- to be able to file the story for that week's edition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So just so that I understand, Mr. Hogg, as soon as the interview was done, you, Mr. Townsley, and the interpreter immediately left and returned to, as you say, the coast. I take it you returned to Split.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You've told us that you recorded this interview.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What did you use to record the interview?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: A small little micro cassette recorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you were interviewed by investigators of this Tribunal, did you provide them a copy of that tape?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, yesterday afternoon we met, and I asked you to listen to that full tape.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the same time, I gave you a copy of a transcript.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us about listening to that tape and reading the transcript.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: The transcript was an accurate but not completely accurate record of what was on the tape. There were a couple of amendments, none of them of a substantive nature. On two occasions I'm supposed to be talking, when in fact it was Simon Townsley talking. The name of a town is -- has been misheard, and that's about it really.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you recognise your voice and Mr. Aziz's voice on the tape?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you also made some pen-and-ink changes to that transcript.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you retained a copy of your pen-and-ink changes.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't have it with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time I would ask that a copy of the transcript be provided to the witness and perhaps he can recall those places where he did make some minor changes. Mr. President, I would ask that this be placed on the ELMO so that the witness can -- everyone can see exactly what the witness is changing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If you could just, Mr. Hogg, for one moment -- we're going to put this on the overhead so that everyone can see exactly what it is that you're changing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Chamber, did -- have the Chamber been provided copies of the transcript? We're on the second page of the transcript, with the last two digits being 4-0.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogg, I see that you've made two markings. Can you please tell us what those two markings that you've made to the transcript are.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah. At the top of the page, where the word was said to have been inaudible I clearly made that out to be "official." So Abdel Aziz was saying: "About myself or my group, it is no allowed to come through any official organisation."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, again, you picked that up listening to the tape?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the second change?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Is there's no such place as Paroba in the next -- when I asked the question: "Is this area basically from Visoko round to Paroba?" It was something beginning with a K but I couldn't make out precisely what, I'm afraid, on the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I believe the other changes were on the page marked 4-8, the last two digits being 4-8.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah. Where I'm supposed to be speaking now, "I have my duty as well to help, and in order to help we need to illustrate the positive action that the Mujahedin are taking," and that was Simon Townsley saying that, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could you please, sir, make that change on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And if you see any other place where you believe it was Mr. Townsley rather than yourself.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I believe that Mr. Townsley said, "But you don't want your face." I don't think that was me, from listening to the tape yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, sir, if you could please make that change.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Hogg, according to my notes, there was one other word that you thought was improperly spelled or transliterated.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah. Sorry. I have to -- to look.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It's actually on the same page, in the lengthy question --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Oh, yeah. In -- sorry about that. Yeah. The usual spelling of "Amphal" is A-m-f-a-l, not P-h-a-l. But I mean, it's a translation from Arabic, so it's open to question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogg, do you recall any other changes or corrections to the transcript based on listening to the tape yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: No. No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time the question arises as to whether Your Honours would like to hear an excerpt from the tape. We do tender both the transcript and the digitised version of the audiotape into evidence at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber deems that it won't be necessary to listen to the tape. As far as the tendering into evidence of the transcript is concerned, the Defence has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence for General Hadzihasanovic, we met with the witness yesterday and we are satisfied that the witness is the person who met with the persons who are mentioned in the transcript, and we don't have any objection to tendering this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We don't have any objections to the admission of this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Mr. Registrar, can we have a number for this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the audiotape gets exhibit number P112, tab 1; and the transcript of the audiotape gets the exhibit number P112, tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, for the record, I am providing the usher with a CD-ROM containing the digital version of the audiotape, which as the registrar said will be P112, tab 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Just to clarify one thing. The Trial Chamber has asked for the position of the Defence with regard to the transcript of this interview. However, you never asked me about the audiotape. However, I wish to say that the Defence does not object to the audiotape being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I would also like to add that the B/C/S version of the transcript gets the exhibit number P112, tab 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I should also note for the record that the witness made the corrections on P112, tab 2 and not on the B/C/S version, P112, tab 3. I would simply point that out for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogg, did there come any time after August 1992 that you returned to Central Bosnia as part of your duties as a correspondent for The Sunday Times?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes. I returned later that year, and in fact spent Christmas that year in Central Bosnia. I then returned to the area twice the following year. It could have been three times. I'm not absolutely certain, but at least twice. In -- from memory, around sort of April time and then around June, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd like to focus your attention on the period of April. I assume that was April 1993?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber where you went in Central Bosnia in April 1993.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Well, I went to various places. The one that really sticks in the mind -- I was only there at that stage for several days at the end of which we pulled out because fighting had erupted in Mostar between the Croats and the Muslim forces. But in the two to three days that I was actually there, I was part of a group of journalists and photographers taken by the British forces in the area in an armoured vehicle up to a village called Miletici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, for clarification, do you know when you say "the British forces," do you know which British forces they were?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: It was the Cheshires, under Bob Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: They were there as part of BritBat.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us why BritBat took you and other journalists in an armoured vehicle to Miletici.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: BritBat at that time was anxious that people back in the UK had a proper understanding of what their role was in Bosnia. One part of their role that they saw was to, because there had in that area also been fighting between Croats and Muslims, on a daily basis they would send out patrols to outlying hamlets to establish what the level of need was in those hamlets or just simply to establish what was happening on the ground. I can't remember why we went to Miletici. I can't -- by which I mean I have no recollection of being told beforehand, "There has been a massacre in this village." My memory is of simply arriving in this village as part of a -- a sort of fairly ordinary British Army patrol and then suddenly discovering that in fact a massacre had taken place there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Trial Chamber what you saw in Miletici and whom you met there on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: There were several elderly deeply distressed Croats. They -- there was a soldier from the Bosnian army who told us that he was there to guard them. The villagers told us that several young men had been killed by the Mujahedin by having their throats slit. We were then -- a house was then pointed out to me called "the white house." I don't know if it was called the white house, but I was told to go and look in the white house. When I walked into the downstairs room, there was a bowl really about a third full of what appeared to be blood, and there was a ladle there, either inside the bowl or beside it. I can't remember which. From memory, the floors -- there was polythene on the floors as well which was smeared with blood. And I was told that the young men of the hamlet, if you like - it was far too small to be called a village really - but the young men had been taken one by one, their heads held above the bowl, their necks slit, and their blood collected in the bowl, which had then been ladled back over their heads as they lay dying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate date that you were in the village of Miletici?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I -- I think it has to have been April. It could have been late March, but I think it has to be April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, for the record, in light of a previous answer, you said: "I think it has to have been April. It could have been late March."

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So sometime in the spring of 1993 [Realtime transcript read in error "1992"].

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: It was in the spring, yeah. It was ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hogg.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has no further questions in direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There may be an error on page 30, line 14, spring of 1992? It should be spring of 1993. The correction has been made. I now give the floor to the Defence, who are preparing to take over. Mr. Bourgon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hogg.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We've had the pleasure of meeting yesterday, yourself plus my colleague Mr. Dixon from the Defence of Mr. Kubura, and myself from -- representing General Hadzihasanovic. But for the record -- and I wish to first of all take this opportunity to thank you for meeting us yesterday.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me begin by introducing myself this morning for the benefit of the transcript. I am accompanied this morning by my colleague, Mrs. Edina Residovic, and my colleague, Mrs. Mirna Milanovic, and my name is Stephane Bourgon, and together we represent General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Hogg, I only have a few questions for you this morning, and I would like to begin simply by confirming that you travelled to Central Bosnia probably twice in 1992; that is, one trip in the fall, when this interview was made, and a further trip around Christmas. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah. The trip when the interview was made was in -- well, I would describe it as the summer really. It was August. Yeah -- no, that's right. I reappeared there sometime sort of late November, early December, and then stayed for some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. And you were further in Central Bosnia probably once in the spring, around April.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you again were in Central Bosnia around June.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if my notes are right, you were in Bosnia and Herzegovina a fifth time in 1994.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But at that time, you did not go to Central Bosnia. You went to Sarajevo only.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, can you confirm that during each of these trips, the aim -- or your personal aim, being, of course, the correspondent for The Sunday Times, that it was to get a story or stories, of course, which would stand out from what would be published in daily papers?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I think that's fair, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the Mujahedin, of course, was such a story that was not a regular in the daily papers.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you can also confirm - and this has been covered by my colleague from the Prosecution - that you did travel in conflict zones before and you had prior knowledge of what were Mujahedins.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: With respect to the first trip in the fall of 1992, I would like to confirm briefly - and we discussed this last night - what was your knowledge in respect of the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I would begin by asking you whether you were aware that in November of 1991 the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna had proclaimed its existence and had claimed to be a separate, distinct, political, cultural, economic, and territorial whole with aims to establishing closer ties with Croatia? Were you aware of this fact?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I wasn't aware, I don't think, of the specifics, of the date, November 1991. I was aware of the fact that the Croats of Herzegovina in many, many cases wanted closer links with Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And were you aware that in January of 1992, which is the day -- the year of your first travel to Bosnia, in January the SDS had proclaimed the Republic of Serbian People with aspiration to join the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I would have been aware of that. Once again, not the specifics of the date, but I knew that that had happened in the very recent past, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I take it you were aware that in April of 1992 the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised as an independent state.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And on the same day it was attacked by the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Which occupied the majority of the territory.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: That's right, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, moving on quickly. Were you aware that on 8th of April, which is two days later, the Presidency of the HZ HB established the HVO as the supreme defence body of the Croatian people in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: No. No. I mean, I was aware that it existed. I wasn't aware of when it was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And were you aware that the constitutional court of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 12th May of 1992 declared illegal the Republic of Serbian People?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: If -- yeah, I wasn't specifically aware of that, no. But I -- I mean, it was a conflict in which things were changing on a daily basis almost, so I'm not surprised to read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And were you aware that on the 14th of September the constitutional court of Bosnia and Herzegovina declared the HZ HB illegal, which of course made the HVO illegal? Were you aware of those facts?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Frankly not. I would assume that the constitutional court was probably sitting in Sarajevo. And if you're in Central Bosnia, you weren't that aware of what was going on in Central -- sorry, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hogg, the -- moving on with the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the government army.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Were you aware that it is only on the 18th of August, 1992 that the Presidency adopted a decision on the establishment of the army which would be divided into five different corps, on the 18th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: All I can say is that when I travelled in -- in Central Bosnia, by the time I was there, there was clearly a Bosnian army in evidence. I had been told prior to my arrival that the first resistance, if you like, to Serb aggression had come from a kind of almost like a territorial army, which -- which seemed almost part time. That wasn't the case when I was there. It had -- an army was -- was apparent.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So I take it, then, that you are not aware either that on the 18th of November is when there was a specific decision to create the 3rd Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which included as part of its area of operations both the Travnik and Zenica municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Right. No, I wasn't aware of that. I -- in Central Bosnia earlier that year, as I've said, there was clearly a Bosnian army. What its structure was, I had -- I had no idea. Certainly when I went back the following year it was very clear that there was something in Zenica called 3rd Corps. I'm not sure that that was clear when I was there in August. I tend to think it wasn't. But there was certainly a Bosnian military structure, whatever its name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And are you aware, based on your last answer, that from this date on - and I'm referring to the 18th of November, 1992, when the 3rd Corps is officially created - that from that point on and during the months that followed, the other -- or the pre-existing structures, including Territorial Defence units, Municipal Defence Staff, and District Defence Staff, were transformed and became subordinate units which were incorporated into the 3rd Corps during that period?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I wasn't aware --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Were you aware of this fact?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I wasn't, no. But it makes perfect sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you are aware that -- you can confirm that when you were in Bosnia in June there was something called a 3rd Corps and you were aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: In Bosnia in June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In June 1993.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you cannot say the same for the period of August 1992 when you were there.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: No, I can't. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, during that trip you mentioned something about a retirement home.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And about speaking to soldiers.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would I be correct to say that although you spoke to those soldiers and they mentioned to you things about Mujahedin, on that particular occasion you did not see any?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any at that -- on that particular occasion at that particular home, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would it all be -- would it be correct to say that these soldiers, when they spoke to you, it was clear in their mind that they were fighting for a civil and secular Muslim nation?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: They made that quite clear to me, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I move on to your second trip, and that is in Easter of 1993.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Right. The third trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sometime in April.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would just like to confirm that you travelled to Miletici and that was with BritBat.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this trip was -- there was no one senior from the British Battalion who accompanied you on this trip.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I don't have any memory of anybody particularly senior, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you are able to confirm -- just hold on there. There appears to be a problem with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Hogg, just to confirm. I asked a question to you, and I would just like to confirm about those soldiers that you met close to the retirement home.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: In the retirement home, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Or in.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What was meant by my question - and I think your answer was yes, but just to make it sure - that these soldiers were telling you that they were not fighting for Muslim fundamentalism.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: My -- my notebook conveys the answers that I was given. One of them said to me, "We're fighting for our lives, our homes, and our children," or something to that extent. What -- Islamic republic? That was clearly in response to a question I would have posed, along the lines of, "What are you fighting for here? Are you fighting for an Islamic republic or a secular state?"

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And your conclusion from this answer was?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: My conclusion from the answer was that they were telling me that they were fighting for a secular state. I didn't necessarily believe what they said, but that's what I was being told.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. And so I come back to the trip in April of 1993. You mentioned the presence of blood that was shown to you.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this would indicate that you were there very shortly after the events which took place in that village?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you confirm that the villagers, when they spoke about who had came into the village, they mentioned to you that those were Mujahedin which did not speak their language.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm not sure they used the word "Mujahedin." They might have -- they might have simply said "foreign fighters" or "Arabs," but yeah, clearly it was Mujahedin they were describing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at that point, Mr. Hogg, I take it that you did not know that shortly before that the bodies of these individuals had been taken away by members of the British Battalion.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I -- I have no memory of -- of being told that in advance, no. It's possible that I was, but I -- like I say, I have no memory of going to Miletici looking for a massacre. I -- I was from memory very surprised at what we found.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can move on to your next trip, which was in June of 1993. We spoke last night, and you mentioned to me another happening when you met Mujahedin in what was quite a scary event.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: That's right, yes. I'd been travelling on the back route between Travnik and Zenica with an interpreter, an Australian Croat interpreter, and we came across a large build-up of the Bosnian army in a sort of small town somewhere along that route. And while passing through them, I noticed a car -- I think it had "TV" emblazoned on the side, which is a normal practice for journalists to do, to stick it up with tape or whatever, in the hope of deterring snipers, et cetera. I then somehow became aware that the people in the car were Bosnian, from Bosnian Television. So my interpreter and I chatted to them about the Mujahedin and we -- myself, the interpreter, and the two guys from Bosnian Television then drove up a hill into the sort of -- a similar area to what -- what looked like Miletici to me, in the sort of foothills of quite a rugged mountain range. And we drove -- parked our cars beside the road and walked across this track into the garden of a house that looked out over a wooded valley, and we -- we were looking for the Mujahedin. The Bosnian camera crew were looking for Mujahedin as well. We met a guy who was Bosnian who was clearly in charge of what was going on at the house. There was a -- a young man giving a call to prayer over the side of the cliff. There was a blanket of some kind on the lawn. I think that there were cherries or something like that, a bowl of cherries or something like that in the middle of the blanket, and there were four or five men, who I frankly at that stage took to be Bosnian, sitting with their Kalashnikovs on the ground. And my interpreter misread the situation. I had no desire that the people that we were with should know that I'd interviewed Abdel Aziz. I wasn't going to be something I'd mentioned. He took it upon himself to tell the chap that we -- who was clearly in command that I was the man who had interviewed Abdel Aziz, at which point the -- the atmosphere changed. He became instantly "hostile" is overstating it, "suspicious" is a better way of describing it. And I remember that suddenly a very large knife was produced and put in the middle of the blanket, which led one of the Bosnian TV men to extract from around his neck under his shirt some kind of -- of Islamic pendant. It might even have been a small locket with copies of the Koran -- with verses of the Koran or something like that. But it was quite clear to me that he had produced this to show all and sundry there that he was a Muslim because he had read the change in atmosphere as rapidly as I had. I immediately denied that I had been the person who had interviewed Abdel Aziz. I said that I'd met him in a hotel in Zagreb and that he had refused to give me an interview, which in fact Abdel Aziz had told me that he had met somebody else in a hotel in Zagreb and that refused to give them an interview. From that point on, my only concern was to get out of there unscathed. I abandoned all hope of trying through this gentleman to reach the Mujahedin. His suspicions were clearly aroused. In talking to him, it was quite clear that mentally he was in a rather odd place. He had returned from Switzerland to join the defence of Bosnia, but he started talking in almost a metaphysical way about the secrets of Islam, and then he started talking in a very threatening way about the existence of fifth columnists who would be killed and they knew and they would be killed. I couldn't quite work out whether he was threatening me at that time and describing me as me a fifth columnist or whether he was talking more generally. As I said, I had only one aim at that precise moment and that was to get into the Lada Niva and leave. And so I-- I accelerated matters, simply thanking him for all his help and suggesting that it was time that we got back to Travnik or wherever it was. We were staying in Vitez actually at that particular time. So we left without incident, but yes, it was unnerving.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hogg. Now, I'd just like to confirm with you that in -- also in June, during that trip, following this scare, you also had a number of people that you met in Central Bosnia, including General Siber, the deputy commander of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I met General Siber in the street in Zenica, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would I be fair to say that you published a story in The Sunday Times on the Sunday, 27th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to present this article. I have a sufficient number of copies for everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] Mr. Hogg, I would ask you to look at this article and to first go to confirm that this is indeed the paper you wrote, which was published on 27th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if the article was published on the 27th of June, 1993, this would mean that the -- most of the material was gathered in the previous two weeks. I think you mentioned to me last night between the 15th and 25th approximately.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: That's right. What I would say though is the inclusion of the material from Miletici -- Miletici was clearly rather earlier. It's depressing to say, but one massacre at that time didn't make a story. And so I hadn't used the material that I had picked up in Miletici up until that period. But when doing a story, you know, two to three months later about Mujahedin atrocities, if you like, then it -- it seemed to me perfectly acceptable to include the material from Miletici.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if you go down just on this paper at the end -- towards the end, there is a paragraph which starts with: "In the hills high Guca Gora."

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: That's right. This is the chap I've just been describing meeting with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's the chap. And that is the event you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Who produced the big knife.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And who said that he was, in terms of, "I am the Hekmatyar of this area."

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And: "I only answer to Allah."

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd just like -- [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should like to tender the article which has been authenticated by the witness, written by him, following the interview that he conducted himself on the ground, and he recognised a particular evident -- a particular event, so I would like to request that this article be admitted into evidence. I have only two more small questions to ask this witness, and then I've finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, regarding this article, which is in the public domain --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, can we have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be DH181.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 10.30. We're going to have the break now, and we will resume after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to give the floor to Mr. Bourgon, whom I interrupted just before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] Sir, I have two questions left for you, the first one being whether you could confirm that you did not know the commander of the 3rd Corps during your travel in 1993 in Bosnia, General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I certainly have no memory of meeting the general, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: It's possible I did, but I have no memory of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you did not know either, Mr. Hogg, the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps, Mr. Merdan, did you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Hogg.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness. [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, the cross-examination is finished on the part of the Defence for General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask the other Defence team whether they have any questions within the scope of their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We do not have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution, do they have any re-examination according to the procedure in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no questions in re-examination, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hogg, I have a number of questions to ask you about the interview that you had with Mr. Aziz and about the period when you were in Miletici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards the interview that you had with Mr. Aziz, you have told us that you had that interview in order to publish an article in The Sunday Times. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: That's right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you said that it was in August that you had this interview, the transcript that we showed to you, the transcript of the audiotape, a few weeks after the interview did you write the article based on this interview?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I wrote the article --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was this article finally published in the newspapers?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I wrote the article. The interview took place on the Thursday, and from memory I think that was August, the 27th. I wrote the article on the Friday, as soon as I got back to Split, and it was published the following Sunday, in The Sunday Times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the article was published, and this article, was it accompanied by any photos? You have told us in response to the Prosecution's question that there was a photographer with you. Did he take any photos during the interview in the month of August? I'm not talking about Miletici and what happened after that.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes. The photographer about two-thirds of the way through the interview, I raised the question of pictures, and after some negotiation Abdel Aziz allowed some photos to be taken of him. He had reservations. He thought that it was un-Islamic. But the photographs were taken and they appeared the following Sunday on the front page of The Sunday Times, one picture of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution could also provide us with the photo and the article. So you confirm that this was published indeed.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before gaining access to this Mujahedin, Aziz, you told us that you had obtained from the army an authorisation, a written authorisation, which allowed you to gain access to this Mujahedin. According to your memory, how was this authorisation drafted? What did it look like? Can you give us any characteristics of this written authorisation? You may not recall. It was a long time ago. But if you can, can you describe this authorisation.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
